claim: NPC1 is a lysosomal membrane protein that exports cholesterol derived from receptor-mediated uptake of LDL.
source: Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) is a lysosomal membrane protein that exports cholesterol derived from receptor-mediated uptake of LDL, and it also mediates cellular entry of Ebola virus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work (e.g., Liscum et al., 1989).

claim: NPC1 mediates cellular entry of Ebola virus.
source: Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) is a lysosomal membrane protein that exports cholesterol derived from receptor-mediated uptake of LDL, and it also mediates cellular entry of Ebola virus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to Carette et al., 2011 and Côté et al., 2011.

claim: Cholesterol export from lysosomes is inhibited by nanomolar concentrations of U18666A.
source: Cholesterol export is inhibited by nanomolar concentrations of U18666A, a cationic sterol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing Ki of 0.03 µM.

claim: U-X, a U18666A derivative with a benzophenone, permits ultraviolet-induced crosslinking.
source: To identify the target of U18666A, we synthesized U-X, a U18666A derivative with a benzophenone that permits ultraviolet-induced crosslinking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figures 5-7.

claim: When added to CHO cells, U-X crosslinked to NPC1.
source: When added to CHO cells, U-X crosslinked to NPC1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was blocked by U18666A derivatives that block cholesterol export.
source: Crosslinking was blocked by U18666A derivatives that block cholesterol export, but not derivatives lacking blocking activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 6B showing competition by compounds B and C but not A, D, and E.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was not blocked by U18666A derivatives lacking cholesterol export blocking activity.
source: Crosslinking was blocked by U18666A derivatives that block cholesterol export, but not derivatives lacking blocking activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was prevented by point mutation P691S in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) of NPC1.
source: Crosslinking was prevented by point mutation in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) of NPC1, but not by point mutation in the N-terminal domain (NTD).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7A showing no crosslinking with P691S mutant.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was not prevented by point mutation P202A/F203A in the N-terminal domain (NTD).
source: Crosslinking was prevented by point mutation in the sterol-sensing domain (SSD) of NPC1, but not by point mutation in the N-terminal domain (NTD).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7A showing normal crosslinking with P202A/F203A mutant.

claim: The SSD of NPC1 contains a U18666A-inhibitable site required for cholesterol export distinct from the cholesterol-binding site in the NTD.
source: These data suggest that the SSD contains a U18666A-inhibitable site required for cholesterol export distinct from the cholesterol-binding site in the NTD.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the crosslinking and mutation data.

claim: Inhibition of Ebola virus entry requires 100-fold higher concentrations of U18666A than inhibition of cholesterol export.
source: Inasmuch as inhibition of Ebola requires 100-fold higher concentrations of U18666A, the high affinity U16888A-binding site is likely not required for virus entry.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to Shoemaker et al., 2013.

claim: The high affinity U18666A-binding site is likely not required for Ebola virus entry.
source: Inasmuch as inhibition of Ebola requires 100-fold higher concentrations of U18666A, the high affinity U16888A-binding site is likely not required for virus entry.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an inference from the concentration differences.

claim: Mutations in NPC1 underlie Niemann-Pick C disease.
source: First, mutations in NPC1 underlie Niemann-Pick C disease, a devastating lysosomal storage disease in which accumulation of cholesterol in lysosomes causes abnormalities in brain, liver, lung, and other tissues, leading to death in the teenage years (Pentchev, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Pentchev, 2004.

claim: Niemann-Pick C disease is characterized by accumulation of cholesterol in lysosomes causing abnormalities in brain, liver, lung, and other tissues.
source: First, mutations in NPC1 underlie Niemann-Pick C disease, a devastating lysosomal storage disease in which accumulation of cholesterol in lysosomes causes abnormalities in brain, liver, lung, and other tissues, leading to death in the teenage years (Pentchev, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Pentchev, 2004.

claim: Niemann-Pick C disease leads to death in the teenage years.
source: First, mutations in NPC1 underlie Niemann-Pick C disease, a devastating lysosomal storage disease in which accumulation of cholesterol in lysosomes causes abnormalities in brain, liver, lung, and other tissues, leading to death in the teenage years (Pentchev, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Pentchev, 2004.

claim: NPC1 is the receptor that permits cellular entry of the RNA genomes of Ebola virus, Marburg virus, and other filoviruses.
source: Second, NPC1 is the receptor that permits cellular entry of the RNA genomes of lethal Ebola virus, Marburg virus, and other filoviruses (Carette et al., 2011; Côté et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Carette et al., 2011 and Côté et al., 2011.

claim: NPC1 mediates the egress of cholesterol that has entered lysosomes through the receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL.
source: NPC1 mediates the egress of cholesterol that has entered lysosomes through the receptor-mediated endocytosis of low density lipoprotein (LDL) (Liscum et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Liscum et al., 1989.

claim: When cell membranes are depleted of cholesterol, LDL receptors bind circulating LDL, internalize it, and deliver it to lysosomes.
source: When cell membranes are depleted of cholesterol, LDL receptors bind circulating LDL, internalize it, and deliver it to lysosomes where acid lipase hydrolyzes the lipoprotein's cholesteryl esters (Brown and Goldstein, 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1986.

claim: Acid lipase hydrolyzes cholesteryl esters in lysosomes.
source: When cell membranes are depleted of cholesterol, LDL receptors bind circulating LDL, internalize it, and deliver it to lysosomes where acid lipase hydrolyzes the lipoprotein's cholesteryl esters (Brown and Goldstein, 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Brown and Goldstein, 1986.

claim: Liberated cholesterol from LDL binds to NPC2, a soluble diffusible protein in the lysosome lumen.
source: The liberated cholesterol binds to NPC2, a soluble diffusible protein in the lysosome lumen (Sleat et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Sleat et al., 2004.

claim: NPC2 transports cholesterol to the lysosomal membrane where it transfers cholesterol to membrane-embedded NPC1.
source: NPC2 transports the cholesterol to the lysosomal membrane where it transfers its cholesterol to membrane-embedded NPC1 (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: The transfer of cholesterol from NPC2 to NPC1 is designated a hydrophobic handoff where hydrophobic cholesterol is shielded from the aqueous environment.
source: Designated a hydrophobic handoff, this transfer occurs in such a way that hydrophobic cholesterol is shielded from the aqueous environment (Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2009.

claim: NPC1 is an intrinsic membrane protein of 1278 amino acids.
source: NPC1 is an intrinsic membrane protein of 1278 amino acids that contains 13 membrane spanning helices separated by hydrophilic loops and 19 potential N-linked glycosylation sites (Davies and Ioannou, 2000) (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Davies and Ioannou, 2000, and shown in Figure 1.

claim: NPC1 contains 13 membrane spanning helices separated by hydrophilic loops.
source: NPC1 is an intrinsic membrane protein of 1278 amino acids that contains 13 membrane spanning helices separated by hydrophilic loops and 19 potential N-linked glycosylation sites (Davies and Ioannou, 2000) (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Davies and Ioannou, 2000, and shown in Figure 1.

claim: NPC1 contains 19 potential N-linked glycosylation sites.
source: NPC1 is an intrinsic membrane protein of 1278 amino acids that contains 13 membrane spanning helices separated by hydrophilic loops and 19 potential N-linked glycosylation sites (Davies and Ioannou, 2000) (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Davies and Ioannou, 2000.

claim: NPC2 transfers cholesterol to the N-terminal domain (NTD) of NPC1.
source: NPC2 transfers its cholesterol to the N-terminal domain (NTD) of NPC1, which is the hydrophilic sequence of 239 amino acids that projects into the lysosomal lumen after the signal peptide is cleaved (Infante et al., 2008a; 2008b).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Infante et al., 2008a and 2008b.

claim: The NTD of NPC1 is a hydrophilic sequence of 239 amino acids that projects into the lysosomal lumen after the signal peptide is cleaved.
source: NPC2 transfers its cholesterol to the N-terminal domain (NTD) of NPC1, which is the hydrophilic sequence of 239 amino acids that projects into the lysosomal lumen after the signal peptide is cleaved (Infante et al., 2008a; 2008b).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Infante et al., 2008a and 2008b.

claim: NPC2 binds to the second luminal loop of NPC1.
source: NPC2 binds to the second luminal loop of NPC1, an event that may precede the cholesterol transfer to the NTD (Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011.

claim: NPC2 binding to the second luminal loop of NPC1 may precede cholesterol transfer to the NTD.
source: NPC2 binds to the second luminal loop of NPC1, an event that may precede the cholesterol transfer to the NTD (Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a speculative statement supported by citation to Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011.

claim: Mutations that abolish the function of either NPC2 or NPC1 lead to cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes and cause Niemann-Pick C disease.
source: Mutations that abolish the function of either NPC2 or NPC1 lead to cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes and cause the fatal Niemann-Pick C disease (Pentchev, 2004; Dixit et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Pentchev, 2004 and Dixit et al., 2011.

claim: Some cholesterol from lysosomes reaches the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: After its transfer to NPC1, cholesterol leaves the lysosome by a mechanism that is poorly understood. Some of the cholesterol reaches the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where it has two actions.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cholesterol binds to Scap in the ER.
source: First, it binds to Scap, an ER protein that regulates the cleavage and activation of membrane-bound sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is established knowledge supported by the Horton et al., 2002 citation.

claim: Cholesterol binding to Scap prevents the protease-mediated release and nuclear entry of the active fragment of SREBPs.
source: Cholesterol binding to Scap prevents the protease-mediated release and nuclear entry of the active fragment of SREBPs, thereby blocking cholesterol synthesis and uptake from LDL (Horton et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Horton et al., 2002.

claim: Cholesterol binding to Scap blocks cholesterol synthesis and uptake from LDL.
source: Cholesterol binding to Scap prevents the protease-mediated release and nuclear entry of the active fragment of SREBPs, thereby blocking cholesterol synthesis and uptake from LDL (Horton et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Horton et al., 2002.

claim: When excess cholesterol reaches the ER, it is esterified with a long chain fatty acid through the action of ACAT.
source: When excess cholesterol reaches the ER, it is esterified with a long chain fatty acid through the action of acyl-coenzyme A cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT), which converts the cholesterol to its storage form as cholesteryl esters (Brown et al., 1975).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Brown et al., 1975.

claim: ACAT converts cholesterol to its storage form as cholesteryl esters.
source: When excess cholesterol reaches the ER, it is esterified with a long chain fatty acid through the action of acyl-coenzyme A cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT), which converts the cholesterol to its storage form as cholesteryl esters (Brown et al., 1975).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Brown et al., 1975.

claim: Lysosome-derived cholesterol reaches the plasma membrane where it fills three distinguishable pools.
source: Lysosome-derived cholesterol also reaches the plasma membrane where it fills three distinguishable pools, thereby assuring membrane integrity (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Das et al., 2014.

claim: NPC1 was identified through a haploid mutagenesis screen to detect genes required for Ebola infection in cultured cells.
source: One group identified NPC1 through a haploid mutagenesis screen to detect genes required for Ebola infection in cultured cells (Carette et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Carette et al., 2011.

claim: Small molecules that block Ebola infection were used with ultraviolet crosslinking to trace their target to NPC1.
source: The other group identified small molecules that block Ebola infection and used ultraviolet crosslinking to trace their target to NPC1 (Côté et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Côté et al., 2011.

claim: Mutant cells that lack NPC1 resist Ebola virus infection.
source: Mutant cells that lack NPC1 were found to resist Ebola virus infection, and infectivity was restored by transfection with a plasmid expressing full length NPC1 (Carette et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Carette et al., 2011.

claim: Ebola virus infectivity is restored in NPC1-deficient cells by transfection with a plasmid expressing full length NPC1.
source: Mutant cells that lack NPC1 were found to resist Ebola virus infection, and infectivity was restored by transfection with a plasmid expressing full length NPC1 (Carette et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Carette et al., 2011.

claim: An Ebola virus surface glycoprotein binds to luminal loop 2 of NPC1.
source: In vitro binding studies demonstrated that an Ebola virus surface glycoprotein binds to luminal loop 2 of NPC1 (Miller et al., 2012), the same loop that binds to NPC2 (amino acids 373–620).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Miller et al., 2012.

claim: Luminal loop 2 of NPC1 binds to NPC2 at amino acids 373–620.
source: In vitro binding studies demonstrated that an Ebola virus surface glycoprotein binds to luminal loop 2 of NPC1 (Miller et al., 2012), the same loop that binds to NPC2 (amino acids 373–620).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Miller et al., 2012.

claim: Ebola sensitivity was restored when NPC1-deficient CHO cells were transfected with a plasmid encoding only the luminal loop 2 portion of NPC1.
source: Indeed, Ebola sensitivity was restored when NPC1-deficient Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells were transfected with a plasmid encoding only the luminal loop 2 portion of NPC1 (Miller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Miller et al., 2012.

claim: NPC1 serves only as the passive attachment site for the Ebola glycoprotein.
source: The latter data indicate that NPC1 serves only as the passive attachment site for the Ebola glycoprotein and that the presumed cholesterol transport activity of NPC1 is not required.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the data that luminal loop 2 alone is sufficient for Ebola infection.

claim: The presumed cholesterol transport activity of NPC1 is not required for Ebola virus entry.
source: The latter data indicate that NPC1 serves only as the passive attachment site for the Ebola glycoprotein and that the presumed cholesterol transport activity of NPC1 is not required.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the data that luminal loop 2 alone is sufficient for Ebola infection.

claim: U18666A inhibits three enzymes in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
source: A powerful tool for the study of lysosomal cholesterol transport and Ebola virus infectivity is an androstenolone derivative termed U18666A that inhibits three enzymes in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Cenedella, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Cenedella, 2009.

claim: U18666A inhibits the exit of LDL-derived cholesterol from lysosomes.
source: In 1989 (Liscum and Faust, 1989) demonstrated that U18666A has another action: it inhibits the exit of LDL-derived cholesterol from lysosomes, thereby creating the equivalent of NPC1 deficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Liscum and Faust, 1989.

claim: U18666A creates the equivalent of NPC1 deficiency.
source: In 1989 (Liscum and Faust, 1989) demonstrated that U18666A has another action: it inhibits the exit of LDL-derived cholesterol from lysosomes, thereby creating the equivalent of NPC1 deficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Liscum and Faust, 1989.

claim: U18666A is a cationic amphiphile owing to a diethylaminoethyl chain attached to the 3-hydroxyl.
source: U18666A is a cationic amphiphile owing to a diethylaminoethyl chain attached to the 3-hydroxyl.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is based on the chemical structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: Other cationic amphiphiles with very different structures also inhibit cholesterol egress from lysosomes.
source: Other cationic amphiphiles with very different structures also inhibit cholesterol egress from lysosomes (Lange et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Lange et al., 2000.

claim: U18666A is more than 100-fold more potent than imipramine at inhibiting cholesterol egress.
source: However, Wojtanik and Liscum (2003) reported that U18666A is more than 100-fold more potent than another cationic amphiphile, imipramine, raising the possibility that U18666A directly inhibits a protein required for lysosomal egress, whereas the low potency amphiphiles may have a nonspecific effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Wojtanik and Liscum, 2003.

claim: U18666A may directly inhibit a protein required for lysosomal cholesterol egress.
source: However, Wojtanik and Liscum (2003) reported that U18666A is more than 100-fold more potent than another cationic amphiphile, imipramine, raising the possibility that U18666A directly inhibits a protein required for lysosomal egress, whereas the low potency amphiphiles may have a nonspecific effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a possibility raised by the potency difference.

claim: Low potency amphiphiles may have a nonspecific effect on cholesterol egress.
source: However, Wojtanik and Liscum (2003) reported that U18666A is more than 100-fold more potent than another cationic amphiphile, imipramine, raising the possibility that U18666A directly inhibits a protein required for lysosomal egress, whereas the low potency amphiphiles may have a nonspecific effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a possibility.

claim: U18666A and other amphiphiles block the cellular entry of Ebola virus RNA.
source: U18666A and other amphiphiles have also been reported to block the cellular entry of Ebola virus RNA (Shoemaker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Shoemaker et al., 2013.

claim: The concentrations of U18666A required to block Ebola virus entry are in the micromolar range.
source: However, the concentrations required are in the micromolar range rather than the nanomolar range at which U18666A blocks cholesterol egress, suggesting that U18666A acts through a nonspecific effect on Ebola virus as opposed to its specific effect on cholesterol transport.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Shoemaker et al., 2013.

claim: U18666A blocks cholesterol egress at nanomolar concentrations.
source: However, the concentrations required are in the micromolar range rather than the nanomolar range at which U18666A blocks cholesterol egress, suggesting that U18666A acts through a nonspecific effect on Ebola virus as opposed to its specific effect on cholesterol transport.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: U18666A acts through a nonspecific effect on Ebola virus as opposed to its specific effect on cholesterol transport.
source: However, the concentrations required are in the micromolar range rather than the nanomolar range at which U18666A blocks cholesterol egress, suggesting that U18666A acts through a nonspecific effect on Ebola virus as opposed to its specific effect on cholesterol transport.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as an inference from the concentration differences.

claim: U-X contains a benzophenone moiety that attaches covalently to proteins when exposed to ultraviolet light.
source: For this purpose, we synthesized U-X, a derivative of U18666A that contains a benzophenone moiety that attaches covalently to proteins when exposed to ultraviolet light (Gubbens et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to Gubbens et al., 2009.

claim: U-X contains an alkyne group that allows attachment of fluorophores and other functional elements through click chemistry.
source: The U-X compound also contains an alkyne group that allows attachment of fluorophores and other functional elements through click chemistry (Kolb et al., 2001; Sapkale et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to Kolb et al., 2001 and Sapkale et al., 2014.

claim: U-X retains the ability to disrupt LDL-mediated cholesterol egress from lysosomes with high affinity.
source: U-X retains the ability to disrupt LDL-mediated cholesterol egress from lysosomes with high affinity.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and demonstrated in Figure 3A showing Ki of 0.06 µM.

claim: U18666A has a Ki of 0.03 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: Compound A has a Ki of 4.5 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: U-X has a Ki of 0.06 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: Compound B has a Ki of 0.01 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: Compound C has a Ki of 0.02 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: Compound D has a Ki of 4.7 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: Compound E has a Ki greater than 10 µM for inhibiting cholesterol esterification in CHO-7 cells.
source: Inhibitory constant (Ki) values denote the concentration at which each compound inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate by 50% in monolayers of intact Chinese Hamster Ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells that were incubated with 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) (mean of 3–14 experiments for each compound).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 legend and the figure itself.

claim: U18666A inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate with high affinity in CHO-7 cells incubated with 10% FCS.
source: Figure 3A shows a cholesterol esterification assay in which 10% FCS was used as a source of LDL-cholesterol. U18666A inhibited the incorporation of [14C]oleate into LDL-derived cholesterol with high affinity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: U-X retained similar inhibitory activity to U18666A in the cholesterol esterification assay.
source: U-X retained similar inhibitory activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Compound A was nearly 100-fold less active than U18666A in the cholesterol esterification assay.
source: On the other hand, compound A was nearly 100-fold less active.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: U18666A did not block cholesterol esterification when stimulated by 25-hydroxycholesterol.
source: In separate experiments, we showed that U18666A did not block cholesterol esterification when it is stimulated by 25-hydroxycholesterol, which enters cells without traversing lysosomes (Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citation to Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009.

claim: 25-hydroxycholesterol enters cells without traversing lysosomes.
source: In separate experiments, we showed that U18666A did not block cholesterol esterification when it is stimulated by 25-hydroxycholesterol, which enters cells without traversing lysosomes (Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citation to Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009.

claim: U18666A does not inhibit cholesteryl [14C]oleate formation when cholesterol is added to ER membranes in vitro.
source: We also found that U18666A does not inhibit cholesteryl [14C]oleate formation when cholesterol is added to ER membranes in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and represents experimental data.

claim: At the lowest concentration tested (0.1 µM), U18666A prevented the reduction in nuclear SREBP-2 caused by FCS addition.
source: In the SREBP-2 cleavage assay, the addition of 10% FCS led to a major reduction in the amount of nuclear SREBP-2 (Figure 3B). At the lowest concentration tested (0.1 µM), U18666A prevented this reduction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: U-X blocked the reduction in nuclear SREBP-2 at low concentrations.
source: U-X also blocked at low concentrations, whereas compound A at 1 µM had no activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Compound A at 1 µM had no activity in blocking the reduction in nuclear SREBP-2.
source: U-X also blocked at low concentrations, whereas compound A at 1 µM had no activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: U18666A and U-X did not inhibit degradation of 125I-LDL.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, U18666A and U-X did not inhibit degradation of 125I-LDL even though both compounds inhibited the lysosomal exit of cholesterol as determined by inhibition of incorporation of [14C]oleate into cholesteryl [14C]oleate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Chloroquine blocked the degradation of 125I-LDL.
source: As a positive control, we incubated the cells with chloroquine, a cationic compound that accumulates in lysosomes where it raises the pH above the optimum for lysosomal proteases and lipases (Goldstein et al., 1975). Chloroquine blocked the degradation of 125I-LDL as well as the release of LDL-derived cholesterol.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Chloroquine accumulates in lysosomes where it raises the pH above the optimum for lysosomal proteases and lipases.
source: As a positive control, we incubated the cells with chloroquine, a cationic compound that accumulates in lysosomes where it raises the pH above the optimum for lysosomal proteases and lipases (Goldstein et al., 1975).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citation to Goldstein et al., 1975.

claim: U18666A acts specifically as an inhibitor of cholesterol export and not nonspecifically as a lysosomotropic agent.
source: These data indicate that U18666A acts specifically as an inhibitor of cholesterol export and not nonspecifically as a lysosomotropic agent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the data in Figure 3C.

claim: Overexpression of NPC1 raised the threshold for U18666A inhibition by more than 100-fold (Ki 0.02 µM vs. 2.7 µM).
source: To test the hypothesis that U18666A targets NPC1, we compared its ability to block the esterification of LDL-derived cholesterol in CHO-7 cells and in TR-4139 cells, a clone of CHO-7 cells that were engineered to stably express excess NPC1 (Figure 4). Overexpression of NPC1 raised the threshold for U18666A inhibition by more than 100-fold (Ki 0.02 µM vs. 2.7 µM).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: TR-4139 cells are a clone of CHO-7 cells engineered to stably express excess NPC1.
source: To test the hypothesis that U18666A targets NPC1, we compared its ability to block the esterification of LDL-derived cholesterol in CHO-7 cells and in TR-4139 cells, a clone of CHO-7 cells that were engineered to stably express excess NPC1 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Overexpression of NPC1 in CHO-K1 cells confers resistance to U18666A as measured by Filipin staining.
source: These quantitative results confirm previous nonquantitative results using Filipin staining to visualize resistance to U18666A in CHO-K1 cells that were engineered to overexpress NPC1 (Ko et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citation to Ko et al., 2001.

claim: Several fluorescent proteins were visualized in a UV-dependent manner in CHO-K1 cells treated with U-X.
source: Several fluorescent proteins were visualized in a UV-dependent manner (Figure 5A, lanes 4–13).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only one fluorescent band at 190 kDa disappeared when cells were incubated with excess U18666A, but not with compound A.
source: Only one of these fluorescent bands disappeared when the cells were incubated with excess U18666A, but not with compound A (lanes 4–6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The apparent molecular mass of the U-X crosslinked protein is 190 kDa, which matches the apparent molecular mass of NPC1.
source: The apparent molecular mass of this protein was 190 kDa, which matches the apparent molecular mass of NPC1 in the same gel system.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 190-kDa band was not seen when NPC1-deficient mutant 10-3 cells were subjected to the U-X crosslinking procedure.
source: The 190-kDa band was not seen when the NPC1-deficient mutant cells were subjected to the same procedure (lanes 7–9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 190-kDa fluorescent band was absent in 10-3 cells but restored when cells were transfected with a plasmid encoding NPC1.
source: Again, we observed that the 190-kDa band was absent in the 10–3 cells (lane 11). It was restored when we transfected the cells with a plasmid encoding NPC1 but not a control protein (lanes 12 and 13).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The transfected NPC1 protein migrated slightly more slowly than native NPC1, owing to the presence of epitope tags.
source: The transfected NPC1 protein migrated slightly more slowly than native NPC1, owing to the presence of epitope tags.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When a control antibody was used in immunoprecipitation, a fluorescent doublet of proteins at about 190 kDa was observed in the supernatant fraction.
source: When a control antibody was used, we observed a fluorescent doublet of proteins at about 190 kDa in the supernatant fraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the presence of anti-NPC1 antibody, the labeled doublet was found in the pellet fraction.
source: In the presence of anti-NPC1, the labeled doublet was found in the pellet fraction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was blocked by U18666A and by compounds B and C.
source: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was blocked by U18666A and by compounds B and C (see Figure 2), all of which contain a dialkylamino group similar to U18666A and all of which block cholesterol exit from lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Compounds B and C contain a dialkylamino group similar to U18666A and block cholesterol exit from lysosomes.
source: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was blocked by U18666A and by compounds B and C (see Figure 2), all of which contain a dialkylamino group similar to U18666A and all of which block cholesterol exit from lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 2 and 6B.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was not inhibited by compounds A, D, and E, which fail to block cholesterol exit.
source: Crosslinking was not inhibited by compounds A, D, and E, which fail to block cholesterol exit (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figures 2 and 6B.

claim: A correctly positioned dialkylamino moiety appended to an androstenolone skeleton is required for achieving a specific block of cholesterol exit.
source: Again, these data emphasize the role of a correctly positioned dialkylamino moiety appended to an adrostenolone skeleton as a requirement for achieving a specific block of cholesterol exit versus a nonspecific lysosomotropal effect of similarly basic compounds, such as A and E.
evidence: This is stated in the Results as an interpretation of the competition data in Figure 6B.

claim: The P691S mutation in NPC1 allows the protein to reach its normal site in lysosomes but prevents it from transporting cholesterol out of the organelle.
source: An amino acid substitution in the membrane region of NPC1 (P691S and P692S in the human and mouse proteins, respectively) allows the protein to reach its normal site in lysosomes, but prevents it from transporting cholesterol out of the organelle (Watari et al., 1999; Ko et al., 2001; Ohgami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citations to Watari et al., 1999; Ko et al., 2001; Ohgami et al., 2004.

claim: The P691S mutation abolishes the binding and crosslinking of [3H]azocholesterol to NPC1.
source: This mutation abolishes the binding and crosslinking of [3H]azocholesterol to NPC1 (Ohgami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citation to Ohgami et al., 2004.

claim: Fluorescent NPC1 was detected in cells expressing wild-type NPC1 after U-X crosslinking, which was competed by U18666A.
source: The cells were incubated with U-X and exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light, after which the bound U-X was tagged with Alexa Fluor 532. After SDS-PAGE, fluorescent NPC1 was detected in cells expressing wild-type NPC1 (lane 3), which was competed by U18666A (lane 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Fluorescent NPC1 was not detected in cells expressing the P691S mutant after U-X crosslinking.
source: Fluorescent NPC1 was not detected in cells expressing the P691S mutant (lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The P202A/F203A mutation abrogates [3H]cholesterol binding in vitro and cholesterol transport in intact cells.
source: Another mutation that abolishes the cholesterol export function is the conversion of two adjacent amino acids in the NTD to alanine (P202A/F203A). This mutation abolishes the binding of [3H]cholesterol (Kwon et al., 2009), and it also reproduces the phenotype of complete NPC1 deficiency when knocked into the mouse npc1 gene by homologous recombination (Xie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citations to Kwon et al., 2009 and Xie et al., 2011.

claim: The P202A/F203A mutation did not prevent crosslinking of U-X to NPC1.
source: However, this mutation did not prevent crosslinking of U-X (Figure 7A, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: NPC1L1 is a close relative of NPC1 that is expressed on the surface of intestinal epithelial cells where it mediates cholesterol uptake.
source: NPC1L1 is a close relative of NPC1 that is expressed on the surface of intestinal epithelial cells where it mediates cholesterol uptake (Altmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citation to Altmann et al., 2004.

claim: U-X did not crosslink to NPC1L1 when expressed in NPC1-deficient 10-3 cells.
source: Figure 7B shows that U-X did not crosslink to NPC1L1 when the latter was expressed in NPC1-deficient 10–3 cells (lanes 13 and 14) as compared to the wild-type NPC1 control (lanes 11 and 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of wild-type NPC1 restored transport of cholesterol derived from LDL in FCS when transfected into NPC1-deficient 10-3 cells.
source: Figure 7C employs the cholesterol esterification assay to show that expression of wild-type NPC1 restored transport of cholesterol derived from the LDL in FCS when transfected into NPC1-deficient 10–3 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cholesterol transport was not restored by transfection of the P691S mutant, the P202A/F203A mutant, or NPC1L1 into 10-3 cells.
source: Transport was not restored by transfection of the P691S mutant, the P202A/F203A mutant, or NPC1L1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The U18666A binding site does not appear to be the same as the cholesterol-binding site in the luminal NTD.
source: Although the precise location of the U18666A binding site is unknown, it does not appear to be the same as the cholesterol-binding site in the luminal NTD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: U18666A does not block binding of [3H]25-hydroxycholesterol to the NTD of recombinant NPC1 in vitro.
source: We earlier showed that U18666A does not block binding of [3H]25-hydroxycholesterol to the NTD of recombinant NPC1 in vitro (Infante et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Infante et al., 2008a.

claim: U-X crosslinked normally to NPC1 bearing a P202A/F203A mutation.
source: Moreover, U-X crosslinked normally to NPC1 bearing a P202A/F203A mutation, which abrogates [3H]cholesterol binding in vitro and cholesterol transport in intact cells (Kwon et al., 2009) (see Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was abolished by the P691S mutation, which lies in the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1.
source: Crosslinking of U-X to NPC1 was abolished by the P691S mutation, which lies in the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The sterol-sensing domain is a segment containing five transmembrane helices (helices 3–7 in NPC1).
source: The sterol-sensing domain is a segment containing five transmembrane helices (helices 3–7 in NPC1) (Nohturfft et al., 1998; Davies and Ioannou, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Nohturfft et al., 1998 and Davies and Ioannou, 2000.

claim: The sterol-sensing domain was initially identified in Scap, the SREBP escort protein that is regulated by cholesterol.
source: This domain was initially identified in Scap, the SREBP escort protein that is regulated by cholesterol (Hua et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Hua et al., 1996.

claim: A similar sterol-sensing domain is found in HMG CoA reductase, another membrane protein that is regulated by sterols.
source: A similar domain is found in HMG CoA reductase, another membrane protein that is regulated by sterols (Hua et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Hua et al., 1996.

claim: Proline 691 is a highly conserved residue that lies in the middle of the predicted third transmembrane helix of the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1.
source: Proline 691 is a highly conserved residue that lies in the middle of the predicted third transmembrane helix of the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is based on structural predictions.

claim: The P691S mutation did not prevent normal localization of NPC1 to lysosomes, but it abolished the cholesterol transport function of NPC1.
source: A mutation that changes this proline to serine did not prevent normal localization of NPC1 to lysosomes, but it abolished the cholesterol transport function of NPC1 (Watari et al., 1999; Ko et al., 2001) (also, see Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Watari et al., 1999 and Ko et al., 2001, and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The P691S mutation prevented the crosslinking of [3H]azocholesterol to NPC1 in intact cells.
source: Moreover, this mutation was also shown to prevent the crosslinking of [3H]azocholesterol to NPC1 in intact cells (Ohgami et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Ohgami et al., 2004.

claim: NPC1 contains a second cholesterol-binding site located in the sterol-sensing domain.
source: Considered together, the data with the P691S mutant is consistent with the idea that NPC1 contains a second cholesterol-binding site located in the sterol-sensing domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the mutation data.

claim: Cholesterol initially binds to the NTD of NPC1 as demonstrated biochemically and confirmed by X-ray crystallography.
source: Cholesterol initially binds to the NTD as demonstrated biochemically (Infante et al., 2008b) and confirmed by X-ray crystallography (Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Infante et al., 2008b and Kwon et al., 2009.

claim: Mutations predicted to disrupt the interaction of NPC2 with the NTD of NPC1 also disrupt cholesterol exit from lysosomes.
source: Mutations predicted to disrupt the interaction of NPC2 with the NTD of NPC1 also disrupt cholesterol exit from lysosomes (Kwon et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Kwon et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2010.

claim: The hydrophobic handoff may be facilitated by the binding of NPC2 to the second luminal loop of NPC1.
source: The hydrophobic handoff may be facilitated by the binding of NPC2 to the second luminal loop of NPC1 (Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative statement supported by citation to Deffieu and Pfeffer, 2011.

claim: NPC2 binding to the second luminal loop may orient NPC2 so that it can transfer cholesterol to the NTD.
source: This binding may orient NPC2 so that it can transfer cholesterol to the NTD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative statement.

claim: Cholesterol may move in relay fashion from the NTD to a second binding site in the sterol-sensing domain.
source: The current data raise the possibility that cholesterol may move in relay fashion from the NTD to a second binding site in the sterol-sensing domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The second cholesterol binding site in the sterol-sensing domain may play a role in transferring cholesterol across the lysosomal membrane.
source: This second site may play a role in transferring cholesterol across the lysosomal membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative statement.

claim: The second cholesterol binding site may lack the exquisite specificity of the NTD, and it may bind U18666A and other cationic amphiphiles.
source: It may lack the exquisite specificity of the NTD, and it may bind U18666A and other cationic amphiphiles that thereby block cholesterol egress from lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative statement.

claim: The postulated cholesterol-binding site in the sterol-sensing domain may require proper membrane orientation in order to bind.
source: The postulated cholesterol-binding site in the sterol-sensing domain may require proper membrane orientation in order to bind.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative statement.

claim: U-X does not crosslink to purified NPC1 in detergent solution.
source: Although U-X crosslinks to NPC1 in intact cells, so far we have been unable to crosslink U-X to purified NPC1 in detergent solution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an experimental observation.

claim: The NTD contains the only site that binds [3H]cholesterol in detergent-solubilized NPC1.
source: Moreover, our previous studies indicated that the NTD contains the only site that binds [3H]cholesterol in detergent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and refers to previous studies.

claim: A single point mutation in the NTD (Q79A) abolished [3H]cholesterol binding to full length NPC1 when the protein was purified in detergents.
source: Thus, a single point mutation in the NTD (Q79A) abolished [3H]cholesterol binding to full length NPC1 when the protein was purified in detergents (Infante et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Infante et al., 2008a.

claim: It is unlikely that binding to the sterol-sensing domain constitutes the mechanism by which U18666A inhibits Ebola virus infection.
source: It is unlikely that binding to the sterol-sensing domain constitutes the mechanism by which U18666A inhibits Ebola virus infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from concentration differences.

claim: Ebola virus inhibition by U18666A requires concentrations (~3–12 µM) that are several orders of magnitude higher than required to block cholesterol transport.
source: According to published data (Shoemaker et al., 2013; Carette et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2012), this inhibition requires concentrations of U18666A (~3–12 µM) that are several orders of magnitude higher than are required to block cholesterol transport (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to Shoemaker et al., 2013; Carette et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2012, and data in Figure 3A.

claim: Ebola infection does not require the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1.
source: Moreover, Ebola infection does not require the sterol-sensing domain of NPC1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and is based on the fact that luminal loop 2 alone is sufficient.

claim: The second luminal loop of NPC1 is sufficient for Ebola virus infection.
source: The second luminal loop of NPC1 is sufficient (Miller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to Miller et al., 2012.

claim: High concentrations of cationic amphiphiles may interact at low affinity with luminal loop 2 of NPC1, thereby blocking virus infection.
source: The data raise the possibility that high concentrations of cationic amphiphiles may interact at low affinity with luminal loop 2 of NPC1, thereby blocking virus infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative interpretation.
